title: SE enablement — reserved vs burst negotiation & fallback runbook (proto)
body:
Purpose:
Quick reference for SEs to negotiate reserved capacity contracts while protecting value for short-term pilots (burst + fallback). Mixes commercial scripts, simple ROI math, technical fallback patterns, and a short checklist SEs can send to procurement/infra teams.

One-liner for customer: "Give your latency-critical paths predictable throughput with Reserved, keep costs low for spikes with Burst, and use Redwood's automatic fallbacks so apps never go cold."

Audience: Field SEs, AE, solution architects, partner sellers. Not a final legal doc — for initial negotiation and discovery.

High-level framing (sales language):
- Problem: Customers need price predictability for their steady-state inference while accommodating unpredictable peaks during launches or seasonal events.
- Redwood answer: Reserved pools for baseline throughput + controlled burst capacity + policy-driven model fallbacks that preserve latency SLOs and cost targets.
- Why it matters: Conserves procurement cycles, reduces surprise cloud spend, keeps product UX consistent during traffic spikes.

Quick facts (one-pagers SE can memorize):
- Reserved: monthly commit, predictable unit price, SLA-backed latency tiers.
- Burst: metered, auto-throttled; configurable cap per account.
- Fallbacks: route by policy — cheaper/quantized model variant, regional fallthrough, or best-effort cached responses.
- Typical econ: <20% extra cost vs on-demand for steady state; burst adds marginal cost only for peak minutes. (Calibrated by workload — see ROI calc below.)

Elevator scripts (30s / 2min / technical):
- 30s: "If you need predictable per-message costs and guaranteed tail latency for critical flows, we reserve GPU capacity for you. For launches and spikes you keep a burst pool so there's no outage — and our routing keeps your top-level SLA intact without overprovisioning."
- 2min: walk through baseline, burst behavior, and a simple example (see ROI). Mention fallbacks and what they mean for output quality.
- Tech: mention KV prefix caching, quantized model variants, and multi-variant routing as real mechanisms to keep latency and cost predictable.

Objections + short counters (copyable):
- "Reserved commitment is risky for us." -> "Start with a low baseline for the pilot (30–90 days), plus documented metrics we monitor together. We provide usage dashboards and can auto-scale commit on agreed signals."
- "How do fallbacks affect output quality?" -> "Fallbacks are policy-controlled and measurable: run fallbacks on non-critical routes first, monitor evals on prompt sets we ship, and use A/B rollout to validate."
- "Procurement wants capex-free." -> "Propose a blended model: small monthly commit + burst with caps; we can convert unused commit into credit for months 2–3 in early pilots. (Legal to approve.)"

Sample ROI (simplified, one-slide numbers):
Inputs: steady QPS = 50 req/s, avg response tokens = 120, on-demand cost per token (hosted) = $0.00015, reserved discounted rate = $0.00009, peak multiplier during launch = 6x for 3 hours, burst metered at $0.00018.
Calculation (monthly):
- Baseline tokens/day = 50 * 120 * 86400 = 518,400,000 tokens/day (note: sanity-check with customer — high token counts are typical of heavy chat).
- Monthly baseline tokens ~ 15.5B.
- On-demand cost/month = 15.5B * $0.00015 = $2,325,000 (example only).
- Reserved cost/month = 15.5B * $0.00009 = $1,395,000.
- Savings = $930k/month (40%).
- Add burst usage: 3 hours * (50*6 - 50) = extra reqs -> incremental token cost at burst price (compute and add).
- Net: reserved + burst often beats pure on-demand for most mid-to-large workloads — show simple % savings on slide.
Notes: always replace numbers with customer telemetry. Keep it high-level in early talks.

Negotiation playbook (step-by-step):
1) Discovery: collect steady QPS, percent of traffic that must meet latency SLO, peak patterns, and procurement constraints.
2) Offer draft: baseline commit (30–90 day pilot), burst cap (daily/hourly), SLA tier, reporting cadence.
3) Pilot approval: include an observability checklist + weekly sync for first 30 days.
4) Scale/renegotiate: after 60–90 days use actual usage to propose a 6–12 month commit with better pricing and convert pilot credits.

Procurement micro-scripts (for AE to send):
- Subject: "Redwood: Pilot commitment & burst cap proposal"
- Body (short): "Hi [procurement], propose a 90-day pilot: baseline commit $X/month (covers steady inference), burst caps of Y tokens/day, and weekly usage reporting. Unused commit in month 1 converted to credits in month 2. Attached: short SOW and usage dashboard sample."

Technical fallback patterns (what to promise, what to avoid):
- Promise: deterministic routing by policy (latency-first, cost-first, regional fallback), ability to pin model versions per route, and informative error codes when fallback choices are applied.
- Avoid promising: identical output quality during all fallbacks; always tie fallbacks to severity (non-critical vs critical routes).
- Implementation notes for SE demos: show a canary where traffic > baseline goes to the fallback path and show latency & token-cost dashboards in console.

Onboarding checklist to attach to pilot SOW (copyable):
- Access: API key + org role for SE + read-only console for customer infra lead.
- Routes: list of routes and traffic percentages to be covered by Reserved vs Burst.
- Eval set: 50 representative prompts for quality regression monitoring.
- Monitoring: set up alert thresholds for 95th/99th latency and token spend burn rate.
- Rollback: define automatic rollback threshold (e.g., >10% quality degradation vs baseline on eval set).

Canary + rollback quickplay (operational):
- Canary steps: 1) Deploy reserved variant for 5% traffic for 24h; 2) Compare token cost and latency traces; 3) If stable, ramp to 25% for 48h; 4) Full swap and start pilot reporting cadence.
- Rollback triggers: sustained latency > SLA for 15m, quality regression > predetermined threshold on eval set, or cost burn > forecast by 25% for 1h.

Short demo script (5–7 minutes):
- Start with console showing traffic pattern and chosen reserved pool.
- Trigger synthetic spike and show fallback route activating and console switching model variant.
- Show per-token cost delta and a cached response path working.
- End with slide: "Next steps: Pilot SOW, ticket to infra for VPC info, initial eval set upload."

Open questions / TODOs for product/legal: (call these out so SEs don't overpromise)
- Can we formalize a credit conversion table for unused commit in pilot months? (Legal)
- Are we comfortable with SLA wording for mixed reserve+burst scenarios? (Legal/SRE)
- Need an example SOW template attached to this doc (Sales Ops).

Attachments to build:
- One-slide ROI template (populate with customer numbers).
- Short SOW/terms template for 30/60/90-day pilot.
- Live demo notebook for showing fallback and cost deltas.

Next steps (for this draft):
- Priya: make ROI slide and share template by EOD Wed.
- Omar: add a short SOW skeleton and get legal comment by next Tue.
- Evan: instrument demo notebook with synthetic traffic pattern by next Fri.
- Maya: iterate doc and move to in_review when above artifacts exist.

Notes to self / SE tips: keep math conservative, avoid micro-promises about quality, use the eval set to quantify tradeoffs. This doc should be shareable with AE and procurement as a starter pack.
